solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: All new flag adopted by diocese (8)

indicatorNotes.adopted by: the diocese takes the new flag into its family, so the diocese goes around it

blocks.note: the cathedral city and diocese of Ely

annotation.surface: A diocese takes on a brand-new banner.
annotation.walkthrough: "Flag" looks like a banner, but here it is the verb meaning to weaken or grow weary.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain adverbial synonym: "all wrong" and "wholly wrong" say the same thing.

entries.clue: Relieved to have stopped short of a century (5)

indicatorNotes.short of: the word is missing its C, so it falls short of that letter

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100, removed

annotation.surface: A batsman is relieved to be out just before reaching a hundred.
annotation.walkthrough: The cricket picture of falling short of a century hides the instruction to drop the Roman hundred.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: pain or pressure that has been lessened has been relieved.

entries.clue: If bad, they would invoke something better (3,5,3,4)

annotation.definition: If bad, they would invoke something better

indicatorNotes.bad: the letters go bad, spoiling into a new order

annotation.surface: When things go wrong, people appeal to something they claim is better.
annotation.walkthrough: The proverb runs "better the devil you know than the devil you don't": when faced with a bad but familiar option, people invoke it as the better choice. The whole clue is the definition, and three of its words are the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the proverb calls a known bad thing better than an unknown one, which is exactly what the clue describes.

entries.clue: No trouble dropping base in concrete (7)

indicatorNotes.dropping base: the base of a down entry is its last letter, which is dropped
indicatorNotes.in: the shortened word goes inside the other

blocks.note: concrete means real, as opposed to abstract
fuss means trouble, bother; lose the last S

annotation.surface: A builder has no difficulty laying a base in concrete.
annotation.walkthrough: "Base" and "concrete" paint a building site, but base is a last letter and concrete is the adjective, as opposed to abstract.
annotation.definitionFit: The noun sense: saying no to a request is turning it down, so a no is a turning-down.

entries.clue: Latin name for German game (5)

blocks.note: Otto is a common German man's name

annotation.surface: A question of what the Romans called a German pastime.
annotation.walkthrough: "German" belongs to the name, not the game: it tells you the name is a German one.
annotation.definitionFit: A game by example: a game of chance like bingo, and the name of many national lotteries.

entries.clue: Break down fences behind hyrax (6)

indicatorNotes.fences: the break-down word fences in, or encloses, the other

blocks.note: an engine that breaks down dies

annotation.surface: An animal breaks down the fences at the back of its enclosure.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fences" looks like a noun but is the verb to enclose, and "behind" is a noun, the backside.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional name: South Africans call the rock hyrax, a small furry mammal, by this Afrikaans word.

entries.clue: Southern state, but not Iowa (7)

indicatorNotes.but not: the state is taken without the letters for Iowa

blocks.note: IA is the US postal abbreviation for Iowa, removed

annotation.surface: A southern US state, as long as it isn't Iowa.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests American states, but the state is a country, and Iowa only supplies its two-letter postal code.
annotation.definitionFit: A formal synonym from Latin auster, the south wind, as in the aurora australis.

entries.clue: Rivers, eg, hold water and guide over channels? (5-2,8)

indicatorNotes.over: the guide word is spread over the channels word, covering it on both sides

blocks.note: an argument that holds water stands up
to con a ship is to steer or guide it

annotation.surface: Rivers are expected to hold water and to flow through channels.
annotation.walkthrough: "Rivers" reads as waterways, but it is Joan Rivers, the American comic.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Joan Rivers made her name telling jokes solo on stage, and "eg" flags her as one instance.

entries.clue: Totally all in? (5,4)

blocks.note: an idiom for completely, as in "___ a king"
read literally: IN is the abbreviation for a unit of length, so this is all of those units

annotation.surface: A question: are they totally exhausted?
annotation.walkthrough: "All in" suggests being worn out, but read literally it is all the INs, and IN stands for inch. The question mark flags that playful reading.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: an idiom meaning completely, and a literal reading of all the units of length abbreviated IN.

entries.clue: Trapper in wonderful drawing (8)

indicatorNotes.in: the trapper sits inside the other word

annotation.surface: A trapper appears in a marvellous picture.
annotation.walkthrough: "Drawing" suggests a picture, but it means attracting, pulling in.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the adjective sense: something that draws or attracts, like a magnet or a charismatic person.

entries.clue: Polar worker following pipe down underwater bank (5)

indicatorNotes.following: the worker comes after the other part

blocks.note: sh is what you say to tell someone to pipe down
Santa's elves work at the North Pole

annotation.surface: A worker in the polar regions follows a pipeline down to the seabed.
annotation.walkthrough: "Pipe down" looks like a pipe laid downwards, but it is the order to be quiet.
annotation.definitionFit: A geographical sense: a ledge of sea floor or sandbank lying under shallow water, as off a continent.

entries.clue: Put one out of school schedule (9)

indicatorNotes.out of: the I is taken out of the word for school

blocks.note: to school is to train; drop the I
I is the Roman numeral one, removed
to slate something is to schedule it

annotation.surface: An instruction to remove a pupil from the school timetable.
annotation.walkthrough: "School" and "schedule" both look like nouns, but both are verbs here.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific sense of put: to put a text into French is to render it in another language.

entries.clue: Lecture on servant’s informal period of work (5-4,6)

indicatorNotes.on: the servant is joined on to the lecture

blocks.note: to dress someone down is to scold them

annotation.surface: A lecture about a servant's casual working hours.
annotation.walkthrough: Man Friday is the servant in Robinson Crusoe, whose name became a byword for a helper. The 's is just surface glue.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: the office custom of letting staff wear casual clothes on the last working day of the week.

entries.clue: Great Britain’s fancy clothing lines (9)

indicatorNotes.fancy: the letters are arranged in a fanciful new way
indicatorNotes.clothing: the rearranged letters dress, or surround, the lines

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for lines

annotation.surface: A fashion-world claim about Britain's stylish lines of clothing.
annotation.walkthrough: "Great Britain" is a false unit: "Great" is the definition, and only "Britain" is shuffled.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the informal sense of excellent, as in "that was great".

entries.clue: One shouts about heading for The Belfry (4,5)

indicatorNotes.about: the shouter goes around the letter
indicatorNotes.heading for: the head, or first letter, of the next word

annotation.surface: Someone yells about heading for The Belfry, the golf venue.
annotation.walkthrough: The Belfry is a famous English golf course, so the surface is about a trip there; the definition is only "Belfry", after "The" has given up its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a belfry is the structure, usually part of a church, where bells hang.

entries.clue: Once framed by Picasso on a shoestring (2,4,2)

indicatorNotes.framed by: the answer sits inside the following words, like a picture in a frame

annotation.surface: A tale of something once framed by Picasso on a tight budget.
annotation.walkthrough: "Once" looks like "formerly" but is the conjunction, as in "once you arrive, call me".
annotation.definitionFit: The conjunction sense: "once he left" means the moment he left.

entries.clue: Duck about to eat wrong plant (5)

indicatorNotes.about: the duck turns about, running backwards
indicatorNotes.to eat: the turned word eats, or takes in, the other

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket

annotation.surface: A duck is about to eat a poisonous plant.
annotation.walkthrough: The duck is not a bird but a cricket score of zero.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a garden flower with tall spikes of pea-like blooms.

entries.clue: See non-clergy turning faithful (5)

annotation.surface: Laypeople converting and becoming believers.
annotation.walkthrough: "Turning faithful" suggests conversion, but the turning belongs to the laity, and "faithful" is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe someone who sticks by a person or cause.

entries.clue: Wiping memory of article in list (7)

indicatorNotes.in: the article goes inside the other word

annotation.surface: Deleting a stored item from a list, as a computer might.
annotation.walkthrough: "List" reads as a catalogue, but it is the verb for a ship leaning over.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary adjective from Lethe, the river of forgetting in Greek myth, so it means causing forgetfulness.

entries.clue: Material set on fire by husband (9)

indicatorNotes.on: the set word is put on after the fire word
indicatorNotes.by: the husband stands by, next to, the rest

blocks.note: to fire someone is to sack them

annotation.surface: Cloth deliberately set alight by a husband.
annotation.walkthrough: "Set on fire" reads as one phrase meaning ignited, but it splits into two separate words, each a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a coarse fabric woven from hemp or jute, worn in mourning or penance.

entries.clue: Red skirts — rip off skirts (7)

indicatorNotes.skirts: the second skirts is the verb: the rip-off word skirts, or goes round the edges of, the other

blocks.note: the first skirts: the skirts of a place are its edges

annotation.surface: A complaint that red skirts are a rip-off.
annotation.walkthrough: The same word does two jobs: the first "skirts" is a noun meaning edges, and the second is the verb for going round.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a deep, rich shade of red with a hint of blue.

entries.clue: Liquid runs — it’s the worst consistency? (15)

indicatorNotes.Liquid: liquid letters flow into a new shape

annotation.surface: Runny liquid has the worst possible consistency.
annotation.walkthrough: "Consistency" looks like thickness, but it means being consistently reliable; the question mark flags the stretch.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose sense, flagged by the question mark: someone consistent in behaviour can be relied on.

entries.clue: Sound horn on top of Harley chopper? (5)

indicatorNotes.on top of: in a down entry, the horn sound sits above the letter; the top of Harley is its first letter

annotation.surface: A biker sounds the horn on a Harley-Davidson chopper motorcycle.
annotation.walkthrough: A chopper is a customised motorbike, but also slang for something in your mouth; the question mark marks the switch.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang: choppers are teeth, so a single chopper is one of them.

entries.clue: Very stuck in one crack (5)

indicatorNotes.stuck in: the V is stuck inside the other word

annotation.surface: Something firmly jammed in a single crack.
annotation.walkthrough: "Crack" reads as a gap, but it is the verb, as in cracking a code.
annotation.definitionFit: The verb sense: cracking a code or a case means finding its answer.

entries.clue: Working on a big new motorhome (9)

indicatorNotes.Working: the letters are worked into a new order

annotation.surface: Someone is fixing up a large new camper van.
annotation.walkthrough: "Working on" looks like one phrase, but "on" is part of the letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A brand name: an American maker of motorhomes, used loosely for any large one.

entries.clue: Small ice art (5)

blocks.note: to ice someone is gangster slang for to kill

annotation.surface: A tiny ice sculpture.
annotation.walkthrough: "Ice art" suggests sculpture, but ice is the gangster verb for murder.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an art, as in the art of conversation, is an acquired knack.

entries.clue: Henley activity, outstanding on river (6)

indicatorNotes.on: the outstanding word is placed on after the river letter

annotation.surface: At Henley, something excellent happens on the river.
annotation.walkthrough: Henley-on-Thames hosts the Henley Royal Regatta, a famous boat race. "Outstanding" means unpaid, not excellent.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the sport of racing boats with oars is what the Henley Regatta is for.

entries.clue: Now then, previously (3,5)

annotation.surface: A speaker's hesitant "now then", followed by a reference to the past.
annotation.walkthrough: "Now then" looks like a single phrase, but "now" is the definition. The two wordplay words join and then split in a different place.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: "for the nonce" means for the present, so the phrase stands for now.
